newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hysan paid a premium on building - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Hysan paid a premium on building - analysts.

text.p: Hysan Development Ltd found a long-sought property investment in Hong Kong's prime Central district but the high cost of the building will weigh on its earnings for some time, analysts said on Friday.

"The company failed to win any of the airport-related property deals they bid for and they needed to do something to boost their earnings base in 1997 and 1998," said Raymond Ngai, senior analyst at UBS Securities.
Hysan has agreed to pay Chinese Estates HK$3.64 billion for the 211,000 square foot, 34-storey Entertainment Building. It will pay a HK$50 million deposit and the remainder in May 1997.
The building has six floors of retail space and 28 floors of office units.

Hysan values the six-floor retail podium higher than the office space. It said the value of the retail space is between HK$20,000 and HK$24,000 per square foot and the office space is about HK$15,000 per square foot.
"The HK$3.64 billion price tag or average per square foot price of HK$17,240 doesn't seem so expensive on that basis," said Raymond Ngai, senior investment analyst at UBS Securities.
Hysan said it expects to raise the current four percent yield, or income earned on the building, to nearly five percent within a short period of time. But analysts are skeptical.

"I don't see rental rates in Central rising much above the HK$63.00 per square foot in 1997," said an analyst with a European brokerage. "I don't think the yield is going to improve that much for them."
The impact of the purchase will have a negative impact on earnings in the second half of 1997, analysts said.
With a yield of four percent and funding costs of about six percent, which leaves Hysan with a negative carrying cost, analysts are revising downward their estimates for the company's 1997 earnings.
"I am likely to revise my earnings forecast down by about eight percent," said an analyst, adding that he was not in favour of the deal.
Prior to the deal, analysts were forecasting 14 percent growth in 1996 earnings to HK$1.4 billion and 17 percent growth to HK$1.65 billion for 1997.

Hysan, which has a strong balance sheet with good liquid assets and little gearing, said it would use a mix of methods to pay for the purchase but could also use 100 percent bank financing without raising its debt to equity ratio above 20 percent.
"The company may sell some low-yielding properties to finance a portion of the purchase as well as bank financing," said Ngai.

But the key to evaluating a company like Hysan is its net asset value and the market is still assessing the impact of HK$17,240-per-square-foot sales price and whether or not it is a benchmark for the Central business district, analysts said.
Prior to the announcement of the deal, Merrill Lynch estimated a net asset value of HK$34.00 for the share and recommended at buy at HK$24.60.
Nomura Research gave a more conservative estimate of HK$30.40 and recommended at buy.
